newsitem.title: USA: "Grumpy old men" at greater risk of heart attack.
newsitem.headline: "Grumpy old men" at greater risk of heart attack.

text.p: "Grumpy old men" are up to three times more likely to suffer from heart disease than their calmer contemporaries, according to a new scientific study to be published on Friday.

The study by a team of Boston scientists involved 1,305 men aged between 40 and 90. The men were categorized in 1986 in terms of their ability or inability to control anger and the scientists tracked their health over following years.
Results showed a direct link between anger and risk -- the higher the level of anger, the higher the risk of the body responding with a heart attack or chest pains.

Even when age and other factors like tobacco and alcohol consumption were factored in, men who scored between five and 14 on the anger scale were 3.15 times more likely to suffer a heart attack than the calmer men, who scored 0 or 1.
"Men who have very violent outbursts of anger are at a greater risk," Dr. Ichiro Kawachi, who led the study team, told Reuters.
Kawachi said men who easily fly into a rage should try to calm down in order to better protect themselves from heart trouble.

"Some people are chronically, excessively and unreasonably angry...For those people, a course of anger management might be helpful," he said -- adding that their families and neighbours might also benefit.

Of the 1,305 men, none of whom suffered from heart disease when the study began, 20 went on to suffer fatal heart attacks, 30 had non-fatal heart attacks and 60 developed angina pectoris, or chest pains caused by heart disease.

None of the almost 200 calmest men suffered fatal heart attacks. There were eight heart attack victims among those who scored two to four on the anger scale and 12 of the angriest group of men were killed by heart attacks.
They were also 1.81 times more likely to have non-fatal heart attacks and 2.44 times more likely to suffer angina pectoris than the mellower men.
The study was to be published on Friday in "Circulation", a journal of the Dallas-based American Heart Association.

The scientists said the exact mechanisms by which anger raises the risk of heart disease are uncertain but that possible factors include the release of stress hormones into the bloodstream, the increased oxygen demanded by heart muscle cells and the added "stickiness" of blood platelets involved in forming clots than can cause heart attack.
